To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

there is no clear evidence of an association between folate intakes or plasma levels and risk of breast cancer, and there is no evidence of an interaction between folate and the MTHFR 677C→T polymorphism in relation to risk of breast cancer.

1) there is no evidence that dietary folate intake is associated with breast cancer risk; 2) there is no association between folatereplete diets and breast cancer risk; and 3) there is no support for the notion that folate intake modifi es the effect of the MTHFR polymorphism in relation to breast cancer risk.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
“ there is limited and inconclusive evidence that higher dietary folate intake is associated with a reduced risk of breast cancer.
dietary folate is not associated with breast cancer risk, although the data are not entirely clear.

the current evidence does not support that dietary folate intake is associated with breast cancer risk, but the evidence for the association between circulating folate levels (as a marker of folate status) and breast cancer risk is limited and inconclusive.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have not found any strong evidence to support the notion that folate intake, either from diet or supplements, has an effect on breast cancer risk.
the evidence is not strong enough to support the use of dietary recommendations or supplements based on genetic susceptibility to breast cancer.

the data do not support a recommendation to increase folate intake as a means of reducing breast cancer risk, nor do they support a recommendation to take folate supplements for breast cancer prevention.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the evidence is not there yet.

the evidence is not yet strong enough for a recommendation that people should be taking folate supplements to prevent breast cancer.
